x: Silver has the lowest resistivity of all metals and is the best conductor. Copper is second, then gold and aluminium.
t: Recall the order silver > copper > gold > aluminium.

x: Option B is incorrect: cadmium sulphide is a compound semiconductor, made of two elements. Silicon and germanium are elemental, and GaAs is a compound.
t: Discriminate elemental from compound semiconductors.

x: Both are true and R explains A: heat breaks more covalent bonds, freeing more electrons and holes, so conductivity rises.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Copper is used in wires, aluminium is light and used in power lines, graphite is the conducting non-metal and electrolytes conduct by ions, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the use or feature of each conductor.

x: I and II are correct: doping adds controlled impurities to raise conductivity. III is false because doping makes an extrinsic semiconductor; a pure one is intrinsic.
t: Discriminate intrinsic (pure) from extrinsic (doped).
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Doping is the controlled addition of impurity atoms to a pure semiconductor.
II. Doping is carried out to increase conductivity in a controlled manner.
III. Doping produces an intrinsic semiconductor.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Silicon's band gap is about 1.1 eV at room temperature. 0.7 eV is germanium's and 4.2 K is mercury's critical temperature.
t: Recall Si 1.1 eV and Ge 0.7 eV.

x: Both are true and R explains A: pentavalent phosphorus has one spare electron that becomes free, making the material n-type.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: A rectifier converts AC to DC, LEDs serve indicators and lighting, a Zener diode regulates voltage, and a photodiode detects light, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the use of each diode type.

x: "Transistor" is short for transfer resistor, since it transfers a signal from a low-resistance to a high-resistance circuit.
t: Recall the origin of the word transistor.

x: I and II are correct: intrinsic material has equal electrons and holes, and n-type has electrons as majority carriers. III is false: in p-type, holes are the majority.
t: Recall the majority carriers in each type.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. In an intrinsic semiconductor, the number of electrons equals the number of holes.
II. In an n-type semiconductor, electrons are the majority charge carriers.
III. In a p-type semiconductor, electrons are the majority charge carriers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Three are insulators: rubber, glass and air. Graphite is the non-metal that conducts.
t: Discriminate insulators from the conducting non-metal graphite.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the Meissner effect is the expulsion of magnetic field, a separate property from zero resistance.
t: Check whether R is a cause or another property.

x: Copper, second only to silver, is the usual wiring metal; aluminium is a light conductor for overhead lines; gold resists corrosion and plates contacts; iron and steel conduct only moderately. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the conductivity grades of metals.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Copper
(b) Aluminium
(c) Gold
(d) Iron and steel

List-II
(i) Second-best conductor, widely used in wiring
(ii) Lightweight good conductor used in overhead power lines
(iii) Corrosion-resistant conductor used on contacts and connectors
(iv) Moderate conductors

x: Both are true: plastic is an excellent insulator, and dry wood insulates well, though wet wood conducts.
t: Recall common insulators.

x: Mica is a mineral that splits into thin sheets used for high-voltage insulation, ceramic insulates at high temperature and dry paper forms the dielectric of paper capacitors, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii.
t: Recall the use of each insulator.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Mica
(b) Ceramic
(c) Dry paper

List-II
(i) Natural mineral that splits into thin sheets for high-voltage insulation
(ii) High-temperature insulator
(iii) Insulating layer in paper capacitors

x: Silicon is the most widely used elemental semiconductor, graphite is a special case, selenium is the elemental semiconductor of early photocells and rectifiers, and lead sulphide is a compound, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Discriminate elemental from compound semiconductors.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Silicon
(b) Carbon in the form of graphite
(c) Selenium
(d) Lead sulphide

List-II
(i) Elemental semiconductor, most widely used
(ii) Special-case semiconductor
(iii) Elemental semiconductor used in early photocells and rectifiers
(iv) Compound semiconductor

x: All three are correct: silicon has atomic number 14 and four valence electrons, and it crystallises in a diamond cubic lattice.
t: Recall the basic facts about silicon.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The atomic number of silicon is 14.
II. Silicon has four valence electrons.
III. Silicon has a diamond cubic crystal structure.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: All four are silicon devices: an IC packs many components on one chip, a solar cell turns sunlight into electricity, a diode conducts one way only, and a transistor amplifies or switches, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall that the code pairs items in order when List-II repeats.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Integrated circuits
(b) Solar cells
(c) Diodes
(d) Transistors

List-II
(i) Many components built on a single silicon chip
(ii) Convert sunlight into electricity
(iii) Allow current to flow in one direction only
(iv) Amplify or switch electrical signals

x: Silicon is the second most abundant element in the Earth's crust, after oxygen.
t: Recall the crust order: oxygen, silicon, aluminium, iron.

x: Germanium has atomic number 32, four valence electrons and a band gap of about 0.7 eV, and it is now used only in special high-frequency and infrared devices, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall the basic facts about germanium.

x: All four are correct: as temperature rises a semiconductor's resistivity and resistance fall, unlike metals, because carrier concentration grows exponentially.
t: Discriminate semiconductors from metals in their temperature behaviour.

x: Both are true: at 0 K a pure semiconductor has no free carriers and insulates, and doping adds carriers, lowering resistance.
t: Recall the effect of temperature and doping on resistance.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the metal fact is just a contrast, while semiconductors' negative coefficient comes from more carriers at higher temperature.
t: Check whether R is about the same material as A.

x: Doping is very light, about one impurity atom per 10⁶ to 10⁸ host atoms, yet it raises conductivity greatly.
t: Recall the doping ratio.

x: Both are true: acceptor (trivalent) doping gives p-type material, and electrons are the majority carriers in n-type.
t: Recall acceptor gives p-type and donor gives n-type.

x: Pentavalent dopants come from Group 15 and trivalent ones from Group 13, boron doping makes p-type silicon, and a donor that releases its electron becomes a fixed positive ion, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall that donors come from Group 15.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Pentavalent dopants
(b) Trivalent dopants
(c) Boron-doped silicon
(d) Fixed ion left behind when a donor atom gives up its electron

List-II
(i) Positive ion
(ii) Group 13
(iii) Group 15
(iv) p-type semiconductor

x: All three are correct: in n-type, holes are minority carriers, and the material stays neutral because fixed positive donor ions balance the free electrons.
t: Recall why doped semiconductors stay neutral.
s:
Consider the following statements:

I. Holes are the minority carriers in an n-type semiconductor.
II. An n-type semiconductor is overall electrically neutral.
III. Positive ions balance the extra electrons in an n-type semiconductor.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: p-type dopants are trivalent and come from Group 13, such as boron, aluminium, gallium and indium.
t: Recall that acceptors come from Group 13.

x: Both are true and R explains A: a trivalent acceptor lacks one electron for bonding, so it accepts an electron and leaves a hole.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true and R explains A: each acceptor that takes an electron becomes a fixed negative ion, balancing the holes, so the crystal stays neutral.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All three are correct: conduction is by free electrons in the conduction band, electrons are negative, and they carry most of the current in n-type material.
t: Recall the role of electrons in conduction.
s:
Consider the following statements:

I. Conduction occurs through free electrons in the conduction band.
II. An electron has negative charge.
III. Electrons provide the main conduction in an n-type semiconductor.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: a hole is a missing electron in a covalent bond, and it acts as a positive charge carrier.
t: Recall the meaning of a hole.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: holes are a minority in n-type because donors add electrons, not because holes move opposite to electrons.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All four are correct: a transistor has two p-n junctions (n-p-n or p-n-p), a heavily doped emitter, thin lightly doped base and moderately doped collector, with the emitter-base junction forward biased and the collector-base reverse biased.
t: Recall transistor doping and biasing.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. A transistor works by current amplification or switching using two p-n junctions, and its two types are n-p-n and p-n-p.
II. The emitter is heavily doped, whereas the base is thin and lightly doped.
III. The collector is moderately doped, and the emitter-base junction is forward biased.
IV. The collector-base junction is reverse biased, and a small input current controls a large output current.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: A transistor amplifier boosts weak signals, a switch gives ON/OFF in digital circuits, an oscillator generates waves, and transistors are the building blocks of ICs, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the roles of a transistor.

x: Both are true: rectifiers are half-wave or full-wave, and a solar cell is a p-n junction that turns light into electricity.
t: Recall diode applications.

x: Diodes give fast switching, clipping and clamping shape waves, and a varactor has voltage-controlled capacitance, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-i.
t: Recall the special uses of diodes.

x: All four are correct: a superconductor is perfectly diamagnetic and works only below a critical temperature, critical magnetic field and critical current density.
t: Recall the three critical limits of superconductivity.

x: Mercury becomes superconducting at 4.2 K, as found by Kamerlingh Onnes in 1911. YBCO and cuprates work at much higher temperatures.
t: Recall mercury as the first superconductor.

x: Both are true: niobium alloys are classic low-temperature superconductors, and high-Tc cuprates work at higher temperatures.
t: Recall examples of superconductors.

x: YBCO (yttrium barium copper oxide) is a high-Tc cuprate superconductor, working above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen.
t: Recall YBCO as a cuprate.

x: All four are superconductor uses: MRI magnets, maglev trains, future lossless power lines and SQUID magnetometers.
t: Recall the applications of superconductors.

x: Both are true and R explains A: germanium's smaller band gap (0.7 eV) lets heat free carriers more easily, so it is more temperature-sensitive than silicon.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true: in p-type material holes are the majority carriers and electrons the minority.
t: Recall the carriers in each type.

x: All four are trivalent Group 13 elements and act as p-type acceptor dopants: boron, aluminium, gallium and indium.
t: Recall Group 13 as acceptors.

x: Germanium leaks more current at high temperature, and it was used in the first transistors and diodes, giving a-i, b-ii.
t: Discriminate germanium's traits from silicon's.

x: LED stands for Light Emitting Diode, a p-n junction that gives out light when forward biased.
t: Recall the expansion of LED.

x: Vacuum, like air, is a natural insulator. Silicon is a semiconductor, and graphite and electrolytes conduct.
t: Classify each material by its conductivity.

x: Graphite carbon is treated as a special-case elemental semiconductor, since it is made of a single element.
t: Discriminate elemental from compound semiconductors.
